title: Atlas of Questions
premise: You are assembling a traveling atlas of how people make, challenge and share knowledge. Visit reconstructed workshops and documentary collections, then use their methods on openly speculative future problems. This is a thematic journey, not a claim that history followed one inevitable ladder. Historical people are not simulated speakers; all requests come from fictional curators.

stages.title: A claim worth testing
stages.speaker: Archive keeper
stages.motivation: Our atlas will travel further than any of us. Before we trust its pages, make a testable question and a repeatable experiment.

area.label: The traveling archive
area.travelText: The atlas travels to the traveling archive; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A claim worth testing: collection
caches.narrative: Field notebooks, measuring tools and drafts from the archive’s teaching collection.

stages.title: Disagreement in the agora
stages.speaker: Debate host
stages.motivation: Two speakers sound equally certain. Give our audience a valid argument and a counterexample that exposes a mistaken generalization.

area.label: An Athenian teaching reconstruction
area.travelText: We are taking what we need with us. The earlier collection remains available behind us.

caches.label: Disagreement in the agora: collection
caches.narrative: A rhetoric teacher’s example claims, diagrams and disputed cases.

stages.title: A book with several pasts
stages.speaker: Alexandrian editor
stages.motivation: Our copies disagree. Prepare a critical edition that preserves the disagreements, and a translation readers can question rather than blindly trust.

area.label: Alexandria’s imagined editorial workshop
area.travelText: The atlas travels to alexandria’s imagined editorial workshop; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A book with several pasts: collection
caches.narrative: The collection contains variant manuscripts, damaged leaves, a bilingual glossary and correspondence.

stages.title: A problem shared across languages
stages.speaker: Mathematics teacher
stages.motivation: Merchants need a fair account, not a mysterious rule. Produce a balanced ledger and a general solution they can use on the next transaction.

area.label: A manuscript workshop in Baghdad
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a manuscript workshop in baghdad; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A problem shared across languages: collection
caches.narrative: Commercial examples, translated mathematical manuscripts, counting tools and geometric diagrams share one desk.

stages.title: Does sight leave the eye?
stages.speaker: Optics curator
stages.motivation: Competing accounts of sight fill these shelves. Build an image-forming model and a repeatable optical experiment we can show visitors.

area.label: An optics workshop in Cairo
area.travelText: The atlas travels to an optics workshop in cairo; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Does sight leave the eye?: collection
caches.narrative: A reconstruction kit holds apertures, screens, lenses, ray diagrams and accounts of experiments.

stages.title: A painted space
stages.speaker: Workshop apprentice
stages.motivation: The patron wants a convincing courtyard, not a rule for every kind of art. Make a perspective drawing and a picture that uses light as well as geometry.

area.label: A Renaissance painting workshop
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a renaissance painting workshop; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A painted space: collection
caches.narrative: Survey sketches, pigments, frames, geometric construction aids and commissions surround a worktable.

stages.title: When the body contradicts the page
stages.speaker: Anatomy curator
stages.motivation: These inherited diagrams deserve careful comparison, not automatic contempt. Make an anatomical atlas and record one correction with its evidence.

area.label: A Padua anatomy collection
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a padua anatomy collection; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: When the body contradicts the page: collection
caches.narrative: Historical plates, comparative specimens, drawing tools and observations from trained anatomists; this is an archive, not a dissection tutorial.

stages.title: How much blood would that require?
stages.speaker: Medical historian
stages.motivation: One explanation says blood is continually used up. Test its quantities against the observations, then assemble a circulation model.

area.label: A collection of Harvey’s questions
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a collection of harvey’s questions; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: How much blood would that require?: collection
caches.narrative: Recorded animal observations, valve diagrams, volume estimates and the competing explanations are laid out together.

stages.title: A changing world in numbers
stages.speaker: Mathematics correspondent
stages.motivation: A falling object and a wandering planet look unrelated. Build a motion model and a method for recovering distance from changing speed.

area.label: Correspondence between mathematical workshops
area.travelText: The atlas travels to correspondence between mathematical workshops; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A changing world in numbers: collection
caches.narrative: Measurements, geometric diagrams and competing seventeenth-century approaches arrive in the archive.

stages.title: The game stopped before the end
stages.speaker: Letter writer
stages.motivation: The players must divide their stake before anyone wins. Find a fair division, then make a risk table that explains more than a single lucky outcome.

area.label: A correspondence table in Toulouse and Paris
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a correspondence table in toulouse and paris; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: The game stopped before the end: collection
caches.narrative: Dice records, unfinished games, payout schedules and copies of the Pascal–Fermat letters.

stages.title: A position that survives the voyage
stages.speaker: Navigation examiner
stages.motivation: The ship needs a position, and the next ship must be able to repeat it. Prepare both a clock-based fix and a lunar-distance fix; compare them at sea.

area.label: Greenwich and the ship’s chart table
area.travelText: The atlas travels to greenwich and the ship’s chart table; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A position that survives the voyage: collection
caches.narrative: Clockmaking parts, astronomical observations, trial logs and navigational tables form a joint test collection.

stages.title: The missing years between two rocks
stages.speaker: Field geologist
stages.motivation: The coast has kept a record with pages missing. Draw the sequence of events and make a deep-time explanation that fits what we can see.

area.label: Siccar Point field collection
area.travelText: The atlas travels to siccar point field collection; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: The missing years between two rocks: collection
caches.narrative: Rock sketches, sediment samples, bedding measurements and competing interpretations from several visits.

stages.title: Resemblance is not a ladder
stages.speaker: Natural-history correspondent
stages.motivation: The specimens vary, and islands have peculiar neighbors. Build an account of branching descent and an explanation of adaptation without a prearranged goal.

area.label: A natural-history exchange
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a natural-history exchange; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Resemblance is not a ladder: collection
caches.narrative: Breeders’ records, island collections, fossil notes and Darwin–Wallace correspondence are compared, not treated as a single author’s revelation.

stages.title: Count the houses, not just the deaths
stages.speaker: Public-health archivist
stages.motivation: Two water supplies serve neighboring homes. Make a fair comparison and a defensible water-safety recommendation, without pretending one map proves everything.

area.label: A London investigation archive
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a london investigation archive; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Count the houses, not just the deaths: collection
caches.narrative: Address records, water-company records, death registers and witnesses’ accounts; the archive includes evidence that complicates the famous pump story.

stages.title: An image others can examine
stages.speaker: Photographic archivist
stages.motivation: A beautiful image is not yet a durable record. Produce a stable photograph and copies that another observer can inspect.

area.label: A nineteenth-century photographic workshop
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a nineteenth-century photographic workshop; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: An image others can examine: collection
caches.narrative: Historical process samples, negatives, optical instruments and preservation records; no chemical preparation instructions are provided.

stages.title: Why did these histories diverge?
stages.speaker: Comparative historian
stages.motivation: A sweeping explanation is tempting. Build a comparison that tests rival explanations and an account that admits what the surviving evidence cannot settle.

area.label: A comparative-history reading room
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a comparative-history reading room; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Why did these histories diverge?: collection
caches.narrative: Travel accounts, trade records, ecological reconstructions and histories written from conflicting standpoints. No single grand theory is supplied as the answer.

stages.title: Send a message through the noise
stages.speaker: Communications engineer
stages.motivation: The link is unreliable. Send a recoverable message, and keep its statistical information distinct from whether it is true.

area.label: A communications laboratory archive
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a communications laboratory archive; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Send a message through the noise: collection
caches.narrative: Message samples, noisy channels, coding diagrams and Shannon’s paper.

stages.title: A result that might not repeat
stages.speaker: Research editor
stages.motivation: A striking result has arrived. Make its uncertainty visible, then prepare a replication that could honestly fail.

area.label: A shared research archive
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a shared research archive; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A result that might not repeat: collection
caches.narrative: Study records, protocols, competing models and unsuccessful replications are preserved together.

stages.title: A resource without a single owner
stages.speaker: Water-users’ secretary
stages.motivation: The canal has several users, each with real needs. Build a workable agreement that can be monitored and revised when it fails.

area.label: A polycentric governance case collection
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a polycentric governance case collection; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A resource without a single owner: collection
caches.narrative: Locally authored rules, monitoring records, user testimony and comparative field studies—not a universal recipe for all societies.

stages.title: A prediction is not a person
stages.speaker: Model evaluator
stages.motivation: A useful model can still mislead the people it affects. Build an evaluated predictor and a way to contest its use.

area.label: A present-day model evaluation workshop
area.travelText: The atlas travels to a present-day model evaluation workshop; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: A prediction is not a person: collection
caches.narrative: Training records, deployment cases, error reports and affected people’s testimony; these are fictionalized research materials.

stages.title: Who may remember for whom?
stages.speaker: Future archive steward
stages.motivation: Our city can preserve experiences across generations. Design a memory archive with consent, then make forgetting possible without erasing everyone else’s evidence.

area.label: Speculative: the intergenerational archive
area.travelText: The atlas travels to speculative: the intergenerational archive; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: Who may remember for whom?: collection
caches.narrative: Imagined preservation tools meet inherited archival practice and unresolved disputes over consent. These are proposals, not predicted inventions.

stages.title: An experiment we cannot undo
stages.speaker: Future assembly recorder
stages.motivation: The planetary proposal promises a great deal. Before anyone authorizes it, make a reversible trial and a decision record that preserves dissent and stop conditions.

area.label: Speculative: a planetary assembly
area.travelText: The atlas travels to speculative: a planetary assembly; earlier objects stay in their previous collections unless still useful.

caches.label: An experiment we cannot undo: collection
caches.narrative: Scenario models, ecological observations and proposals from several jurisdictions meet the archive you have assembled.

sources.title: Siccar Point: geological evidence and Hutton
sources.note: Hutton used an unconformity to support an existing account of repeated geological processes; one scene does not establish every feature of his theory.

sources.title: NLM: Andreas Vesalius
sources.note: The Fabrica both relied on and corrected Galen. This is not a rejection of every inherited account.

sources.title: OU primary-book exhibition: Harvey
sources.note: Harvey used quantitative, experimental, analogical and teleological arguments. Recipes isolate questions rather than reconstruct his whole reasoning.

sources.title: Royal Museums Greenwich: Harrison and longitude
sources.note: Chronometers and lunar distances coexisted. Sea trials, cost and reproducibility matter alongside invention.

sources.title: National Gallery: perspective
sources.note: Linear perspective is one historically specific representational practice, not the culmination of all painting.

sources.title: Oxford History of Science Museum: mathematics in Islamic cultures
sources.note: Practical problems, inherited mathematics and original contributions cross languages and regions. No exclusive origin claim.

sources.title: Pascal–Fermat correspondence, 1654
sources.note: The interrupted-game problem is a case study, not the first human reasoning about chance.

sources.title: Cambridge: Newton Principia manuscript
sources.note: Mathematical recipes are modern teaching models; they do not assert the Principia was written in modern calculus notation. Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently.

sources.title: Darwin: On the Origin of Species, first edition
sources.note: Historical primary text, not endorsement of every nineteenth-century claim; natural selection is not inevitable progress or a moral rule. Wallace is a parallel contributor.

sources.title: UCLA: Snow’s grand experiment
sources.note: Compare water companies and denominators, not merely dots on a map. Observational comparisons have limitations.

sources.title: UCLA: Broad Street outbreak context
sources.note: Do not claim a map alone revealed the cause, or pump-handle removal alone ended an already declining outbreak.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Talbot and photography
sources.note: Several processes and contributors; a reproducible negative differs from a unique direct-positive image. No chemical procedure is taught.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
sources.note: Information-theoretic quantities do not measure truth, significance or wisdom.

sources.title: Elinor Ostrom: Beyond Markets and States
sources.note: Institutional design is contextual; neither markets, states nor commons automatically solve every collective-action problem.

notes: Research/content draft, not independently judged fun or live-site content.
220 distinct combinations. Only successful combinations count; moving, placement, reading and stage advances are separate.
All combinations express an authored teaching model, not necessary/sufficient historical causation.
Stages deliberately avoid arbitrary choose-N quotas. Goals identify actual products.
Current draft uses documentary areas rather than mechanical locations. Real catalyst trials are a planned revision, not faked by marking every workshop a catalyst.
No terminal item vanishes automatically. Retirement must be explicitly justified in a future revision; current draft retires nothing.
Sources support selected chapter facts, not every recipe. Chapters with no sources remain authenticity-review candidates.
Future chapters are speculative institution design, not predictions or claims of inevitable progress.
